findings.title: Transaction signing for 1 chain(s) relies on elliptic-curve signatures
findings.description: The wallet's message definitions cover Solana. These chains authorize transactions with Ed25519, which Shor's algorithm breaks on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. A wallet cannot move a chain to post-quantum signatures on its own: the chain has to adopt a scheme first.
findings.impact: Once a CRQC exists, an attacker who sees an account's public key could derive the private key and move funds; how soon keys are exposed depends on each chain (address reuse, account model).
findings.recommendation: Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them. Keep the signing layer crypto-agile per chain (algorithm identifiers in messages and storage, room for larger keys and signatures) and track each chain's post-quantum proposals, so that a new scheme can be added when a chain activates it.
findings.retest: Re-run when a chain activates a post-quantum signature scheme or the wallet adds one.
findings.limitations: This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Chains are recognized from the names of the message definitions (.proto files and packages); the schemes are the chains' documented account signatures, not an analysis of the wallet's signing code.
findings.method: Message definitions (.proto) matched to QSI's table of chain signature schemes.
findings.repro: Open the .proto files named in the evidence.

findings.title: TLS without a post-quantum key exchange: rustls before 0.23 (ring only)
findings.description: rustls before 0.23 (ring only) at Cargo.toml:289: the configured key exchange (ring) has no hybrid ML-KEM group such as X25519MLKEM768 (RFC 10024), so the handshake cannot negotiate one.
findings.impact: Traffic protected only by classical ECDHE could be recorded today and decrypted once a CRQC exists (harvest now, decrypt later). Relevant when transmitted data must stay confidential for many years.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade rustls to 0.23 or later with the aws-lc-rs provider and the prefer-post-quantum feature.
findings.retest: Connect with a client that offers X25519MLKEM768 (openssl s_client -groups X25519MLKEM768 with OpenSSL 3.5+, or a Go 1.24+ client) and confirm the negotiated group.
findings.limitations: This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Read from code and manifests only: the library versions deployed and settings made outside the code (environment, launch flags) were not determined.
findings.method: Static reading of TLS library configuration in code and manifests: crypto provider, group and curve lists, GODEBUG.
findings.repro: Open Cargo.toml:289 and inspect the quoted lines; the evidence lists further files.

pq.assumptions: Planning assumptions: x for key establishment, x for signatures, y are the defaults of the risk profile “Small technology company”, not the client's figures; with the client's actual lifetimes the verdict can change.

roles.label: channel key exchange (TLS, Noise, handshakes)
roles.action: Move the handshake to a hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3; a hybrid KEM in Noise-based protocols)

roles.label: threshold signing and MPC protocols
roles.action: Track post-quantum threshold signatures (NIST IR 8214C) and keep the protocol layer ready to swap the signature scheme; record which keys and shares must stay valid for how long

roles.label: transaction and message signing
roles.action: Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them

roles.label: role not determined
roles.action: Classify each usage, record data lifetimes, and plan migration to ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), in a hybrid/composite form where the ecosystem supports it; introduce an abstraction layer for crypto-agility

maturity.label: no post-quantum cryptography
maturity.next: Inventory where classical public-key cryptography protects long-lived data and keys, and choose the first migration: usually a hybrid TLS key exchange and wrapped keys.
facts: Classical only — channel key exchange (TLS, Noise, handshakes): TLS (classical groups) (1 file(s))

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — factoring
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Breaks RSA at every key length: a longer modulus only raises the cost polynomially. Plan migration to ML-KEM (or a hybrid) for key establishment and ML-DSA / SLH-DSA for signatures; start with keys protecting data that must stay confidential for years (harvest now, decrypt later) and with long-lived signatures.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Needs a fault-tolerant quantum computer. Published estimates for RSA-2048 fell from 20 million noisy qubits and 8 hours (Gidney–Ekerå 2021) to under a million noisy qubits and under a week (Gidney 2025); a 2026 neutral-atom design puts RSA-2048 one to two orders of magnitude slower than P-256 on 26,000 qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions; no such machine is publicly known.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — discrete logarithms in finite fields
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Breaks finite-field Diffie–Hellman and DSA at every size. Move key establishment to ML-KEM (hybrid with X25519 or ECDH during the transition) and signatures to ML-DSA or SLH-DSA.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Gidney–Ekerå (2021) estimate RSA and finite-field discrete logarithms together; the resources are of the same order. Ekerå–Gärtner (2024) compare the current algorithm variants for safe-prime and Schnorr groups.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: 2026 estimates for a 256-bit curve: under 1,200 logical qubits and 90 million Toffoli gates, under half a million physical superconducting qubits running for minutes (Babbush et al.); 1,193 logical qubits with more gates (Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher); P-256 in a few days on 26,000 neutral-atom qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

quantum_algorithms.name: Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: The search is long and serial: NIST counts AES-128 key search as 2^170/MAXDEPTH quantum gates with MAXDEPTH between 2^40 and 2^96 and uses it as the yardstick of security category 1; a SHA-256 preimage was estimated at about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits (Amy et al. 2016).

quantum_algorithms.name: Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: 256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Bernstein (2009) argued that, once hardware cost is counted, it is not cheaper than classical parallel collision search; NIST defines security category 2 by SHA3-256 collision search counted in classical gates (2^146).

scenario.rationale: Between the 10-year band (28-49%) and the 15-year band (51-70%): roughly where the experts' averaged likelihood crosses one half. More than half of the respondents (13 of 26) already put the likelihood at 50% or more for some horizon.
